title: Bold outside, careful inside
hookLine: be confident about outside things and cautious about your own judgments (Discourses 2.1)

lines: THE DEER RUN INTO THE NETS.
cards: Hunters in the ancient world had a clever trick for catching deer. They'd string a line of feathers across the woods.

The feathers fluttered, the deer panicked and ran the other way, straight into the nets the hunters had set. The deer weren't cowards. They were afraid of the wrong thing, and fearless about the wrong thing.
Epictetus thought most of us live exactly like those deer.

teach.b: Book two of the Discourses opens with chapter one: that confidence isn't at odds with caution. The Stoics claimed you should be both, completely bold and completely careful, and people thought that sounded like nonsense.

teach.h: CAREFUL WHERE THE REAL DANGER IS.
teach.b: Be careful where the real danger is: in your own will. That's where you can actually go wrong, by agreeing too fast, wanting the wrong thing, acting on a bad impression.
And be bold about everything outside the will, because nothing out there can make you bad. Then he shows how we flip it.
We're terrified of things outside us, death, exile, pain, losing face, and reckless inside, quick to agree with any thought that comes along.

teach.h: WE FLIP IT, LIKE THE DEER.
teach.b: Like the deer, fleeing the feathers into the nets. He has another image for the outside fears. Death and pain, he says, are like the masks that scare little children.
Turn the mask around and look at the back. It doesn't bite.

What frightens us is mostly our opinion about death and pain, not the things themselves. This doesn't mean being careless with your health or safety; Epictetus would still have you look both ways crossing the street.
It means putting your carefulness where it does the most good, on your own judgments, and letting your courage go out into the world.

how: Stoic readers often use this chapter to sort their fears, acting boldly on outside things they've been avoiding while slowing down their own quick judgments.

o: brave in public, even if you feel scared inside
acting tough so that others won't see your fear
bold about outside things, careful with your judgments

games.q: bold outside, careful inside: tap the pairs.
p: turn it around; it doesn't bite

s: Epictetus says confidence and caution can't go together
he says be confident about outside things and cautious about your own will.
he compares death and pain to masks that frighten children
turn the mask around and you'll see it doesn't bite.
Epictetus says to be careless about your health
he means placing caution where it matters most, on your judgments.

games.q: you're a deer in the woods. a line of feathers flutters ahead of you. what do the deer in Epictetus' story do?
o: flee the feathers and run into the nets.
games.why: they fear the harmless feathers and run straight into the real danger, the way we fear outside things and grow careless within.

practice: Think of one outside thing you've been avoiding out of fear, a phone call, a conversation, speaking up, and turn it around like a mask: what's actually on the back? Usually it's discomfort, not disaster.
Then turn inward to one judgment you made too fast, and hold both: bold out there, careful in here.

wordCard.voice: Bold outside. Epictetus' answer to the Stoic paradox: be confident about what's outside your will, and save your caution for your own judgments.

orig.note: Greek tharsos: confidence, boldness; paired in Discourses 2.1 with eulabeia, caution.

carryVoice: Your line: turn the mask around. The back of it doesn't bite. That's day four hundred seven.
